scenes.title: Call them to you

briefing.type: Earthquake, shop fronts and awnings collapsed
briefing.access: From the Willis Street end, on foot
briefing.number: About 3 casualties here, more reported further along
briefing.emergencyServices: Fire and Emergency NZ and Hato Hone St John 10 minutes out

localHazard.found: Glass from the shop window is scattered around the fallen shelf; you sweep a clear patch before you kneel.
localHazard.injury: You kneel on a shard of window glass and cut your knee.

expected.credit: Looked up at the awnings and shop fronts before going in.
expected.miss: You went in under the damaged shop fronts without checking for danger.

teaching: Call out 'If you can walk, come to me' before you go to anyone. Everyone who walks is green, and you only sieve the people left behind.
Walking is the first step of the sieve. A graze, a limp or a hand held to an arm does not change it.
Someone who does not answer may not have heard you. Beckon, point and mime walking before you decide they cannot follow instructions.
Green is green for now, not for good. Note the mechanism on the card and re-triage walkers when you have time.
The woman who stays put is trapped under a shelf. She cannot walk, so she is next on your sieve.
Glass, loose stock and leaning shelves can hurt you too. Look before you kneel, even beside someone who is calling for help.

scenes.title: One try, then black

briefing.type: Earthquake, shop front and cafe ceiling collapsed
briefing.emergencyServices: Fire and Emergency NZ and Hato Hone St John 15 minutes out

localHazard.found: Loose bricks from the shop front are stacked against his shoulder; you ease them clear before you kneel.
localHazard.injury: A loose brick slips off the pile and hits your hand.

bystanders.description: Man in a work jacket who found the casualty and is shaking
lines: I found him like this! Please, pump his chest!

expected.credit: Checked the damaged shop front and cafe ceiling before going in.
expected.miss: You went in under loose masonry and a broken ceiling without checking for danger.

events.description: The man who found him shouts at you to start CPR.

teaching: Open the airway once, then look, listen and feel for breathing for the full check.
Still not breathing after one airway opening means tag black, even though it feels wrong.
Do not start CPR in a mass casualty incident. It ties you to one casualty while others you can save wait.
A black tag is not giving up. It lets you reach the woman calling for help under the beam.
A bystander begging for CPR is understandable. Say briefly why you are moving on, tag black and keep going.
A look up and around takes five seconds, even for someone you expect to tag black. A rescuer hurt by falling masonry helps nobody.

scenes.title: Stop the bleed first

briefing.type: Earthquake, shop front collapsed onto the footpath
briefing.emergencyServices: Fire and Emergency NZ and Hato Hone St John 10 minutes out

localHazard.found: Glass from the shop window is scattered around him; you sweep a space clear before you kneel.
localHazard.injury: You kneel straight onto a shard of window glass and cut your knee.

expected.credit: Looked up at the broken shop front before kneeling beside him.
expected.miss: You went in without looking up at the broken shop front.

teaching: Catastrophic bleeding is the first question in the sieve. Stop it before you check anything else.
A tourniquet goes high on the thigh, above the wound, and is tightened until the bleeding stops. Write the time on the card.
Shouting does not mean he is fine. Pale, sweaty skin and a fast pulse point to heavy blood loss.
Once the bleed is controlled, tag red and move on. Do not stay to comfort him or give a drink.
Look for glass, wires and loose stock before you kneel. Five seconds now is cheaper than a hurt rescuer later.

scenes.title: Cannot follow a command

briefing.type: Landslide onto the coast road, two vehicles hit
briefing.hazards: Further slips, rockfall, heavy rain, wet road, traffic in the open lane
briefing.access: From the north, one lane open along the verge
briefing.emergencyServices: Hato Hone St John from Kaikōura 20 minutes out, Fire and Emergency NZ 25 minutes

localHazard.found: Loose rocks and slip mud are banked against her side; you move the rocks clear before you touch her.
localHazard.injury: A rock rolls off the mud bank and hits your shin.

expected.credit: Looked up at the slope and along the road before anyone knelt on the verge.
expected.miss: You went onto the slip without looking at the slope above.

expected.credit: A lookout watched the slope and the traffic was slowed before you worked beside the open lane.
expected.miss: Nobody watched the slope or slowed the traffic while you worked beside the open lane.

teaching: Breathing and pulse can look fine in a casualty with a serious head injury. The command check is what finds it.
A casualty who breathes but cannot follow a simple command is red.
Put her in the recovery position to protect her airway, then move on.
The woman with the bleeding scalp talks and obeys, so she is orange. A dramatic scalp wound is not a red tag.
Quiet is not safe. The casualty who is not making a noise is often the one who needs you first.
On a slip, post a lookout and agree a signal before you work. Three short whistle blasts mean leave the area now.

scenes.title: Children breathe faster

briefing.type: Earthquake, classroom block ceiling and roof beam collapsed
briefing.access: Through the school gate off High Street
briefing.emergencyServices: Fire and Emergency NZ 10 minutes out, Hato Hone St John 15 minutes

localHazard.found: A sheet of ceiling board hangs loose above the beam; you keep out from under it and work from his side.
localHazard.injury: The loose ceiling board comes away and hits your shoulder.

override.approach: Teenage girl in a school uniform sitting in the school courtyard, wincing with a hand pressed to her chest, her left lower leg bent out of line.
override.mechanism: Thrown against the edge of a desk when the earthquake shook the classroom block.

bystanders.description: Teacher in a lanyard, pale but steady
lines: That's Hemi, he's nine. He's been stuck under that beam for over an hour.
The older girl is Grace. She's fourteen.

expected.credit: Looked up at the sagging ceiling before going into the classroom block.
expected.miss: You went into the damaged classroom block without checking for danger.

teaching: Children have their own breathing limits in the sieve. In the child sieve only a rate under 15 or over 45 is red.
Hemi breathes 42 to 44 times a minute. That is orange in a child, but the same rate would be red in an adult.
At 14, Grace goes through the adult sieve, where more than 30 breaths a minute is red.
Being trapped does not change the category. Sieve Hemi as normal, then flag him for medical before anyone frees him.
The teacher can give you names and ages. Ask her rather than questioning a frightened child.
Look up before you go in. A classroom with a broken ceiling can shed more on you while you work.

scenes.title: Do not lift it off

briefing.type: Earthquake three hours ago, office building floors collapsed
briefing.access: From Lichfield Street, through the cordon
briefing.number: 1 casualty trapped, more may be inside
briefing.emergencyServices: Fire and Emergency NZ urban search and rescue and Hato Hone St John medics 15 minutes out

localHazard.found: Loose rubble is packed under the edge of the slab; you keep your weight off that side and kneel at his head.
localHazard.injury: Rubble shifts under your knee and you lurch against the slab edge, bruising your arm.

bystanders.description: Man in a hard hat from the building next door
lines: We'll just lift it off him! Give me a hand!
He's been stuck for hours, we can't leave him!

expected.credit: Checked the floor and the load above him before going in.
expected.miss: You went in under a collapsed floor without checking for danger.

events.description: The man in the hard hat grabs the edge of the slab and tells you to help him lift it.
Control: a medical team and a rescue crew are 15 minutes away. Hold any release until they arrive.

teaching: Trapped but breathing normally, with a pulse and following commands, is orange.
After hours under a heavy load, lifting it off can release toxins into the blood and stop the heart.
Flag for medical before any release. Do not free him yourself and do not let a well-meaning bystander try.
However thirsty he is, nothing by mouth.
Tag orange, write on the card how long he has been trapped, and move on.
One long whistle blast means stop work and keep quiet so the search team can listen. Wait for the resume signal before you start again.

scenes.title: The quiet one

override.approach: Man sitting on the footpath beside a collapsed shop front, shouting and moving about, holding his left forearm, which is visibly bent.
override.mechanism: Fell as the shop awning came down in the earthquake, landing on his left arm.

override.approach: Man lying still on his back on the footpath in front of a collapsed shop front, eyes closed, with a cut on his head and bruising on his face.
override.mechanism: Struck by falling masonry from the shop front when the earthquake hit. A passer-by saw him go down and he has not spoken since.

localHazard.found: Glass and chips of masonry lie around his head; you brush them clear before you reach in.
localHazard.injury: You rest your palm on a piece of broken glass and cut it.

expected.credit: Looked up at the shop fronts before going in under them.
expected.miss: You went in under the damaged shop fronts without checking for danger.

events.description: The man with the bent arm shouts for you again: 'Hey! Over here! My arm!'

teaching: The loudest casualty is rarely the sickest. Go to the quiet one first.
A casualty who is quiet and cannot follow a simple command is red, even when the breathing rate and pulse look fine.
The man with the bent forearm shouts but can walk, so he is green. Do not splint his arm in the first sweep.
A breathing casualty who is not obeying goes into the recovery position to keep the airway open.
Look at everyone before you commit. The quiet casualty is easy to walk past while others shout.
Check overhead before you kneel under a damaged shop front. Glass can follow the masonry down.

scenes.title: Panic is not an injury

briefing.exactLocation: Tsunami evacuation point, Bluff Hill, Napier
briefing.type: Tsunami surge on the Marine Parade, evacuation under way
briefing.hazards: Further surges, floating debris, crowding on the track
briefing.emergencyServices: Hato Hone St John and Police 15 minutes out, Civil Defence centre opening

localHazard.found: The grass beside her is a slick, muddy slope churned up by the crowd; you dig your boots in and kneel on firmer ground.
localHazard.injury: Your boots slide on the wet slope and you go down on one knee, jarring your wrist.

expected.credit: Checked the crowded track and the footing before going in.
expected.miss: You went in without checking the crowded, muddy track for danger.

events.description: The woman grabs your sleeve and tries to drag you toward the water: 'I have to get out! Let me go!'

teaching: Panic is not an injury. If she can walk, she is green.
Give one short, firm instruction, such as 'Walk to the green area', instead of staying to calm her.
Fear can push the breathing rate to 28 to 30, but the walking step comes first and she is green.
The quiet woman on the grass is the one to worry about. Confused and not following commands makes her red until she can.
Do not stay with the panicking person. Ask a walking casualty to take her to the green area.
Crowds and wet, steep tracks are dangers too. Check your footing before you kneel.

scenes.title: Not who shouts loudest

briefing.type: Tour coach rolled onto its side on a bend
briefing.access: From the north, along the verge
briefing.number: About 2 casualties here, more on the bank
briefing.emergencyServices: Fire and Emergency NZ and Hato Hone St John 20 minutes out

override.approach: Elderly man sitting on the gravel verge beside the overturned coach, restless and anxious, holding his head where there is a small cut with a little bleeding, his left lower leg bent at an odd angle.
override.mechanism: Thrown from his seat when the coach rolled. He hit his head and twisted his left ankle.

localHazard.found: Diesel is seeping from the coach beside the wheel; you step round it and kneel on dry ground.
localHazard.injury: You kneel in the diesel and it soaks through your trousers; you stop to wipe yourself down.

bystanders.description: Older woman in a green cardigan, Eru's wife
lines: Eru first, please! He's hurt his head!
You can't just walk past him!
Why are you going to her? He needs you!

expected.credit: Cones out, hazard lights on and a lookout posted before anyone worked beside the road.
expected.miss: Nobody slowed the traffic: casualties were treated beside passing vehicles.

events.description: Mere grabs your arm: 'Eru first, please! He's bleeding from his head!'
Mere pulls you back as you turn away: 'You can't leave him! Stay with him!'

teaching: A bystander's urgency is not a triage category. Sieve in the order you find people, not the order you are told.
Eru takes a short sieve: not walking, breathing rate normal, pulse fine, obeys commands. That is orange, and you move on.
The quiet woman slumped by the wheel is pale and sweaty with no blood in sight. Expose and look: a bleed under a heavy jacket needs a tourniquet in seconds.
Expose and look takes 15 seconds. A full head-to-toe check takes three minutes.
Do not argue. A calm 'I will be back for him' is enough, then carry on.
Cones and a lookout come before casualties on a live road.

scenes.title: Safety first

briefing.exactLocation: Builders' supplies store, Hutt Road, Petone
briefing.type: Earthquake, mezzanine floor collapsed in the store
briefing.hazards: Aftershocks, cracking brick wall, falling stock
briefing.access: Through the loading bay on the east side
briefing.emergencyServices: Fire and Emergency NZ and Hato Hone St John 10 minutes out

localHazard.found: Stacked timber and boxes lean over his head from the broken mezzanine; you move the loose ones clear before you kneel.
localHazard.injury: A box slides off the leaning stack and hits your shoulder.

override.approach: Woman sitting on the ground beside the collapsed mezzanine with a length of steel reinforcing bar sticking out of her right thigh. She is sweating and shouting: 'Don't touch it!'
override.mechanism: Fell from the edge of the mezzanine onto a length of steel reinforcing bar stacked below when the floor gave way in the earthquake.

expected.credit: Checked the cracked wall and the leaning stock before going in.
expected.miss: You went in under a cracked wall and a broken mezzanine without checking for danger.

events.cue: The floor jolts under you and the stacked timber along the wall starts to rattle and sway.
events.followUpCue: The shaking stops. A fresh crack runs up the brick wall above you and fine dust is sifting down.
events.description: A strong aftershock hits. The brick wall above you cracks and dust pours down.

teaching: Check for danger first, and keep checking. A scene that looks safe can change in seconds.
When the ground shakes or a wall cracks, withdraw to safety straight away. You cannot help anyone if you are hurt.
Do not finish the casualty you are with first. Withdraw within seconds, report to Control and return when the area is cleared.
Leaving casualties is hard, but a rescuer who is injured becomes another casualty.

scenes.title: Tourniquets do not fit the groin

briefing.hazards: Loose metal panels, wet floor, noise
briefing.access: Through the main gate, then the loading dock
briefing.emergencyServices: Hato Hone St John 8 minutes out, Fire and Emergency NZ 10 minutes

localHazard.found: The torn metal sheet that cut him lies edge-up on the floor beside him; you slide it clear before you kneel.
localHazard.injury: Your glove catches the torn edge of the metal sheet as you reach in and you cut your hand.

bystanders.description: Factory worker in a hi-vis top and hard hat, calm
lines: He's my workmate. Tell me what to do.
I can hold it, just show me where.

expected.credit: Had the dryer isolated and the loose panels cleared before you worked beside it.
expected.miss: Nobody confirmed the dryer was isolated: you worked beside the failed equipment and loose panels.

events.description: Control: ambulance is 8 minutes out. Tell them about the groin bleed when they arrive.

teaching: A tourniquet does not work on the groin. There is no limb segment above the wound for it to sit on.
Pack the wound and press hard. The groin, neck and armpit are junctional areas.
Ask the worker to hold firm pressure while you finish the sieve checks, then tag red.
He is shouting, pale and sweaty, which means heavy blood loss. Stop the bleed first, tag second.
Make sure the machinery is isolated before you work beside it. Ask the site staff to confirm, and do not take it for granted.

scenes.title: Open the airway first

briefing.access: From the Featherston side, along the verge
briefing.number: About 1 casualty here, more further down
briefing.emergencyServices: Fire and Emergency NZ and Hato Hone St John 20 minutes out

localHazard.found: Pieces of broken window glass lie in the grass under her; you pick out the larger ones before you kneel.
localHazard.injury: You kneel on a piece of coach window glass and cut your knee.

bystanders.description: Man in a jacket crouched by the casualty, shaking
lines: I found her like this. She hasn't moved. Is she dead?

expected.credit: Cones out, hazard lights on and a lookout posted before you knelt on the verge.
expected.miss: Nobody slowed the traffic on the pass: you knelt beside passing vehicles.

events.description: The man beside her tells you she is dead and there is nothing to do.

teaching: Always open the airway before you decide someone is not breathing. A blocked airway can look exactly like death.
Breathing that starts after the airway is opened is red, and opening the airway was the life-saving step.
Settle her in the recovery position before you move on, or the airway can close again.
A bystander saying she is dead is not a triage assessment. Check for yourself.
In the sieve the airway comes before spinal care, so a collar can wait for the treatment team.
Cones, hazard lights and a lookout come before you kneel on a live road, even for someone who is not breathing.
